items.title: How Taxes Work in the U.S.

blocks.md:
Taxes are money people and businesses pay to the government. They pay for things we share, like roads, schools, the military, parks and programs like Social Security.

**Common kinds of taxes**
• **Income tax:** on money you earn. Paid to the federal government, and in most states, to the state too.
• **Payroll taxes:** for Social Security and Medicare. They come out of each paycheck.
• **Sales tax:** added when you buy things in most states.
• **Property tax:** paid by people who own homes or land.

**Your first paycheck**
Your pay before taxes is **gross pay**. What you actually get is **net pay**. The difference is taxes and other deductions.
**Parent tip:** Show your teen a real pay stub. Walk through gross pay, each tax and net pay together.

**Withholding**
When you start a job, you fill out a **W-4** form. It tells your employer how much tax to hold back from each paycheck.

**Tax brackets**
The US uses brackets. Each slice of income is taxed at its own rate. Moving into a higher bracket only raises the rate on the dollars in that slice, not all your income.

**Marginal vs effective rate**
• **Marginal rate:** the rate on your last dollar earned
• **Effective rate:** your total tax divided by your total income. It's always lower than your top rate.

**Filing a tax return**
Each year, usually by mid-April, you file a return. If too much was withheld, you get a **refund**. If too little, you **owe** the difference.
**Try this:** Use the bracket tool in Module 2. Move the slider and watch the effective rate stay below the top rate.

question.prompt: You move into a higher tax bracket. What happens?
options: All your income is taxed at the higher rate
Only the income above the line is taxed at the higher rate
question.hint: Brackets work like stairs, not a cliff.
question.explanation: Only the dollars above the bracket line get the higher rate. Earning more never lowers your take-home pay because of brackets.

items.title: Taxable income
items.md: Income left after deductions. Tax is figured on this.

items.title: Marginal rate
items.md: The rate on your last dollar earned.

items.title: Effective rate
items.md: Total tax divided by total income.

items.title: Withholding
items.md: Tax taken out of each paycheck ahead of time.

blocks.md:
Both lower your taxes, but in different ways.

**Deductions** lower your taxable income.
Most people take the **standard deduction**, a set amount everyone can subtract. Others list their deductions one by one, called itemizing.

**Credits** lower your tax bill directly, dollar for dollar.

**Which is worth more?**
Say your tax rate is 12%.
• A $1,000 deduction saves about $120.
• A $1,000 credit saves $1,000.

**Credits you may hear about**
• Earned Income Tax Credit
• Child Tax Credit
• American Opportunity Tax Credit, for college costs

Rules and amounts change, so check IRS.gov or a tax pro for the current year.

question.prompt: Which saves more: a $1,000 tax credit or a $1,000 deduction?
question.hint: One cuts your tax bill, one cuts your taxable income.
question.explanation: A credit cuts your tax by the full $1,000. A deduction only saves your tax rate times $1,000.

blocks.md:
Some accounts give you a tax break for saving.

**Retirement accounts**
• **Traditional 401(k) or IRA:** you may get a tax break now and pay tax later when you withdraw
• **Roth 401(k) or IRA:** you pay tax now, and qualified withdrawals later are tax-free

**Health Savings Account (HSA)**
If you have a qualifying health plan, an HSA can give tax breaks for medical costs.

**Tips for a first job**
• Fill out your W-4 carefully
• Keep your pay stubs and the **W-2** form you get in January
• Even if you don't owe tax, filing may get your withheld money back
• Free filing help is available at IRS.gov

**Plan all year**
Taxes aren't just an April thing. Small choices during the year add up.
